## The Problem

I had a card worth hundreds of dollars in deals and barely used it, because finding what was actually near me took longer than just going to my usual spot.

The Starving Student Discount Card bundles 400+ deals from businesses across Provo and Orem for BYU/UVU students, but the official app organizes everything as a flat category list, with no map. Chains with multiple locations get split across categories or duplicated, so it's unclear whether two listings are the same business or different ones. With no way to see what was actually nearby, I rarely used a card I'd already paid for.

## What I Built and Why

I built a mobile-first PWA that puts all 418 deals on an interactive map instead of a list. Nearby pins cluster together so a chain with nine locations doesn't flood the screen, and tapping a cluster spiders the pins out for an exact pick. I added category filters, a nearest-first sort that only asks for location permission after explaining why instead of throwing a native browser prompt at someone cold, and a usage tracker so I can see at a glance how many uses I have left before a deal is exhausted. It runs off a static dataset with no backend, since the data doesn't change often enough to justify the added complexity.

I ran user testing with classmates in my 490R course early on, which surfaced UI friction I couldn't see myself and shaped a more intuitive layout. Since that first version I've kept iterating: cross-device sync, a favorites tab, a rewards tab, and a swipe-to-redeem flow with a countdown screen so marking a deal used feels deliberate instead of an easy misfire.

## How It Went

It fixed exactly the problem I built it for. I went from barely opening the official app to actually checking the map before deciding where to eat, since the deals nearest me show up immediately instead of being buried in a long list.

## What I'd Do Differently

The data cleanup ended up being a much bigger lift than the UI. There are six separate geocoding and data-cleaning scripts plus multiple manual review CSVs in the repo. If I started over, I'd plan for that as its own phase up front instead of discovering mid-build how messy 199 businesses' addresses actually were.

## Tech Stack

Vite, React 19, react-leaflet (OpenStreetMap), Tailwind CSS, Firebase/Firestore, vite-plugin-pwa
